opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really important distinction, and people tend to blur the two together. When most folks hear "AI improving itself," they picture the recursive loop where a model is literally generating data, designing experiments, and kicking off training runs that produce a better successor model. That's improvement across generations. The thing doing the improving and the thing being improved are different artifacts, and the gains get baked into weights.

What I'd call improvement within the same medium is different. The model's weights are frozen, but the system around it gets better: the prompts, the scaffolding, the tools it writes for itself, the memory it accumulates, the code it uses to orchestrate its own work. If you have an agent that rewrites its own harness, or builds up a library of skills and heuristics in text or code, it gets measurably more capable at a task without anyone touching the underlying model. It's improving in the medium it already operates in, which is language and code, rather than in gradient space.

The way I'd draw the line in practice comes down to where the improvement lives and how durable and general it is. Weight-level improvement tends to generalize broadly and persist, but it's slow, expensive, and hard to inspect. Within-medium improvement is fast, cheap, and legible. You can read the prompt or the code diff and see exactly what changed, and roll it back. But it's often narrower and bounded by the base model's capability ceiling. You can only scaffold your way so far.

What's interesting is that the second kind is happening right now, at scale, and probably gets underrated because it doesn't fit the dramatic "intelligence explosion" narrative. And the two feed each other. The artifacts agents produce within the medium, like better traces, better tools, and better evals, become exactly the training signal for the next generation of weights. So I think of them less as competing paths and more as an inner loop and an outer loop.

r001.rationale: It describes within-medium artifacts feeding into the next generation of model weights, with the two improvement paths feeding each other as inner and outer loops. This communicates autocatalytic, cross-media improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is there are really two very different loops that people lump together when they say "self-improving AI."

The first one is the one everybody imagines: the model trains a better version of itself. It's writing the training code, picking the data mixture, running the experiments, and at the end of the loop there's a new set of weights that are better than the old ones. That's improvement by changing the substrate. The thing doing the work is literally a different artifact than the thing that started the loop.

The second one is improvement within the same medium, and I actually think it's the more interesting and underrated one right now. The weights don't change at all. What changes is everything around the weights. The model builds itself better tools, it writes better scaffolding, it accumulates notes and memory, it figures out a better harness for the task, it decomposes problems into subagents more effectively. Same model, same forward pass, but the system as a whole gets meaningfully more capable over time because the environment it's operating in has been shaped by its own previous work.

The reason I think the distinction matters is that they have totally different dynamics. The weight-training loop is expensive, slow, and hard to verify. Every iteration costs you a training run, and it's genuinely difficult to tell whether the new model is better or just different. The in-medium loop is cheap and fast, and it's auditable. You can read the tool the model wrote. You can diff the prompt. You can look at the memory file and say, okay, that's wrong, delete it. A human can stay in the loop without it being a bottleneck.

A useful mental test I use: if you swapped the model out for a fresh copy with the original weights, how much of the improvement survives? If most of it survives, that's in-medium improvement. The gains live in the artifacts, not the parameters. If almost none of it survives, then the gains were baked into the weights, and that's the self-training kind.

And honestly, most of what I'd call real recursive improvement today is the first kind. People talk about the weights loop because it sounds like the sci-fi version, but the day-to-day compounding we're actually seeing is a model making its own workspace better and then being more effective in it tomorrow.

r001.rationale: The response describes feedback loops in which a model improves its workspace or trains new weights, but it does not characterize system-assisted self-improvement across different media as autocatalytic improvement.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish those by asking where the improvement lives. If an AI system trains a new model, it’s changing the weights—you end up with a different model that’s hopefully more capable. But a system can also improve while keeping the underlying model fixed: it can write better tools, change its prompts, accumulate useful memories, or revise how it approaches a task.

That’s what I mean by improvement within the same medium. The system is working through code or text, and the improvements are themselves code or text that it can use on the next iteration. You can get a compounding loop there without running another training job. The important question is whether those changes actually make it better, and whether it has a reliable way to tell.

r001.rationale: The response describes compounding improvement through code or text without another training job, but does not characterize system-assisted self-improvement across different media as autocatalytic improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between improving the model and improving the system around the model. If an AI generates training data, runs experiments, and trains a better successor, the improvement ends up in new model weights. That’s one kind of self-improvement.

But you can also keep the weights fixed and have the system write better tools, change its instructions, or develop a better way of organizing its work. Then the improvement lives in code, memory, or the workflow it uses. You’re improving within the medium the system already operates in.

The interesting question is whether those improvements compound: does each change make the system better at finding and evaluating the next change? That’s a stronger claim than simply having an AI help train another model.

r001.rationale: The response describes improvement across model weights and system-level code, memory, or workflow, then characterizes compounding as changes that help the system find and evaluate further changes—an autocatalytic improvement loop.
